story: The Paparoa Range, the backdrop to the park, is ancient granite shaped by ice into its rugged outline. Limestone underlies most of the rest, and it makes the landscapes the park is known for: high coastal cliffs, river canyons, delicate cave formations, and at Dolomite Point near Punakaiki the 'pancake-stack' rocks, where the sea forces water and air up through caverns below to burst from the blowholes. They perform best at high tide in a south-westerly swell.

The mild coastal climate and fertile soils grow varied forest. Near the coast broadleaf forest rules, with glades of nīkau palms that give it a subtropical feel and big rātā emerging above the canopy; inland, hard, red and silver beech mix with rimu and other podocarps. Tūī, bellbird/korimako and kererū move between coastal and upland forest with the seasons. South of the Punakaiki River is the only known breeding place in the world of the Westland petrel/tītī, which in the breeding season can be seen flying to and from the colony at dusk and dawn.

The coast was rich in mahinga kai, food from the sea, rivers and forest, and lay on the traditional travel route along Te Tai Poutini, the West Coast, one of the few places pounamu could be found. Ngāi Tahu, led by Te Pare and Tūhuru, won control of these lands from Ngāti Wairangi in a series of conflicts whose final defeat came at Paparoa. Today Te Wao Nui, the great forest of the park, is a taonga to Ngāi Tahu and Ngāti Waewae.

A large national park extending north and east of the Paparoa Range was proposed in 1979 and rejected, but after years of submissions 30,327 hectares were gazetted as Paparoa National Park on 23 November 1987. It has grown since, with land added in 2002 under the Forest (West Coast Accord) Act and in 2015, when, at the families' wishes, the Pike River mine site, where an explosion killed 29 men on 19 November 2010, became part of the park.
howItWorks: Paparoa is run by the Department of Conservation (DOC), with a visitor centre at Punakaiki. DOC says there are no fees for entry into the park or for a day walk or ride on the Paparoa Track; under the National Parks Act 1980 the public has freedom of entry and access. The one charge most day visitors meet is for parking: DOC's car park at the Punakaiki Pancake Rocks charges by the half hour, paid by card at the machines.

The Paparoa Track is a Great Walk shared by walkers and mountain bikers: 55 kilometres over three days on foot, or two by bike. Its three Great Walk huts, Ces Clark, Moonlight Tops and Pororari, must be booked in advance, and there are no campsites on the track. Huts have bunks, mattresses, heating, gas cooktops, toilets and water, but no food, utensils or showers. A Backcountry Hut Pass is accepted at Ces Clark Hut but not at the other two. E-bikes are banned under the park's management plan, and riding at night is not allowed, to protect nocturnal wildlife.

Dogs are not allowed in the park, and flying a drone needs a DOC permit. At the Pancake Rocks you may not climb on the rocks, which shelter nesting birds and rare lepidium plants; keep to the path and behind the barriers. Much of the inland country is wild and untracked, with hidden holes and caverns, so keep to the tracks.

sightNotes.poi-nz-paparoa-pancake-rocks-and-blowhol: Layered limestone stacks, surge pools and blowholes at Dolomite Point, on a 30-minute paved loop mostly suitable for wheelchairs. Best at high tide with a south-westerly swell.
sightNotes.poi-nz-paparoa-truman-track: A 30-minute return walk from the highway north of Punakaiki through nīkau forest and flax to platforms above a wild beach and a waterfall off sandstone cliffs.
sightNotes.poi-nz-paparoa-pororari-river-gorge: A limestone gorge with huge boulders and deep pools, a lookout 15 minutes from the road, and the walkers' entry to the Paparoa Track. Rockfall: don't linger in the gorge.
sightNotes.poi-nz-paparoa-ballroom-overhang: A huge limestone overhang up the Fox River, with a toilet and room to camp. A demanding 4-hour return with unbridged river crossings; avoid after rain.

entrances: Punakaiki and Dolomite Point, on State Highway 6 — the Pancake Rocks, the visitor centre and the short coastal walks
Pororari River car park, 1 kilometre north of the visitor centre — the walkers' end of the Paparoa Track
Smoke-ho car park near Blackball, the start of the Paparoa Track
Pike29 Memorial car park at the end of Pike Valley Road, by a narrow gravel road unsuitable for buses and long campervans
The Fox River car park, 12 kilometres north of Punakaiki, for the Inland Pack Track and Ballroom Overhang
planYourVisit.reservations: Paparoa Track huts must be booked in advance; bookings for 2026/27 are open. You will need somewhere to stay the night before you start, because camping at Smoke-ho car park is not permitted.
permits: A DOC permit to fly a drone
Annual parking permits for the Pancake Rocks car park, bought online
camping: No campsites on the Paparoa Track
Ballroom Overhang can be used as a sheltered overnight camp
lodging: Ces Clark, Moonlight Tops and Pororari Great Walk huts on the Paparoa Track
Accommodation at Punakaiki, Greymouth and Westport
seasonalClosures: Heavy rain can make the Pororari River Track, the Inland Pack Track and the Fox River crossings impassable; Bullock Creek Road often floods
In winter check snow and ice conditions on the tops of the Paparoa Track before you go

chronology.text: Ngāi Tahu migrate to Te Waipounamu in the mid to late 17th century and later win the West Coast, with a final victory at Paparoa.
A track is built up the Pororari valley for a planned settlement; the Paparoa Track follows parts of it.
A large national park extending north and east of the Paparoa Range is proposed; it is rejected.
Paparoa National Park, 30,327 hectares, is gazetted on 23 November and declared open on 5 December.
On 28 April a DOC viewing platform above Kotihotiho/Cave Creek, near the park, collapses, killing 13 students and a DOC officer.
About 7,450 hectares are added under the Forest (West Coast Accord) Act 2000.
On 19 November an explosion at the Pike River mine kills 29 men.
At the families' wishes, the Pike River mine site and surrounding land become part of the park.

safety: Rivers can rise fast and many crossings are unbridged. Do not cross a flooded river; turn back or wait for it to drop. If in doubt, stay out.
At the Pancake Rocks keep to the path: straying beyond the barriers is very dangerous, and the return track comes out suddenly on the highway, so keep children close.
The beach at the end of the Truman Track has serious hazards; read DOC's warnings before going down to it.

Rockfall can occur in the Pororari gorge, and hunters may be in the Pororari area. The Paparoa Track and Pike29 Memorial Track are steep and exposed for riders; the tops can be far colder than the car park.
Follow the Land Safety Code from DOC and the NZ Mountain Safety Council: choose the right trip, understand the weather, pack warm clothes and extra food, share your plans and carry a distress beacon.
regulations: No drones without a DOC permit.
No climbing on the Pancake Rocks; stay on the formed path and behind the barriers.
Paparoa Track huts must be booked; no camping on the track or at Smoke-ho car park.
No e-bikes on the Paparoa Track, and no riding at night.

weather: The weather comes in off the Tasman Sea. DOC's management plan describes the coast as mild and humid, with little change through the year, and the spine of the Paparoa Range as wet and often wrapped in mist; snow never reaches the lower parts of the park in winter. Cold katabatic winds flow down from the range into the Pororari River and Bullock Creek valleys. Heavy rain can arrive with little warning, and on the tops of the Paparoa Track expect rain, fog, high wind and, in winter, snow and ice. Rivers rise quickly, so check the forecast and river conditions before any walk with crossings.
directions: Paparoa lies in the north of the South Island's West Coast, along State Highway 6 between Westport, 55 kilometres north of Punakaiki, and Greymouth, 43 kilometres south. InterCity buses run a regular service along the coast, and the nearest airport with scheduled flights is at Westport. There is no petrol station in Punakaiki, so fill up in Westport or Greymouth. The Paparoa Track starts at Smoke-ho car park near Blackball and ends near Punakaiki: walkers finish at the Pororari River car park, riders at the Waikori Road car park. The Pike29 Memorial Track is reached from Greymouth by Taylorville Road, Taylorville–Blackball Road and Atarau Road, then Logburn Road to the end of Pike Valley Road.
